name: The Triangle Inequality
statement: The length of any side of a triangle is at most the sum of the lengths of the other two sides.
meaning: For a triangle with sides a, b, and c, each side is bounded by the sum of the other two. Abstractly, in a normed space the norm of u + v is at most the norm of u plus the norm of v, and in a metric space the distance from A to C is at most the distance from A to B plus that from B to C. It formalizes that a direct path is never longer than a detour.
mechanism: The straight segment between two points is the shortest path, so going through an intermediate point cannot be shorter. For norms, it follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality by expanding the squared norm of u + v and bounding the cross term. Equality requires the points to be collinear, with the vectors on the same ray.

examples.text: Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 20, states that in a triangle the sum of any two sides is greater than the remaining one.
It is one of the defining axioms of a metric space, ensuring distances behave consistently: the distance from A to C is at most the distance from A to B plus that from B to C.
A corollary, the reverse triangle inequality, bounds the difference of two norms by the norm of their sum, useful for estimating differences of lengths.

whyItMatters: It is the axiom that makes "distance" meaningful across geometry, analysis, and topology, and it is essential for defining metric and normed spaces. Countless convergence and continuity proofs rely on chaining it.
limits: It holds for genuine norms and metrics; equality occurs only in the degenerate, collinear case — a zero-area triangle with vectors on the same ray. Distance-like functions that violate it, such as squared Euclidean distance, are not true metrics.
misreadings: The strict version (strictly greater) holds only for non-degenerate triangles; the general statement uses "at most" to include the collinear case. It bounds a side by the sum, not the difference, of the other two.
origin: Known since antiquity; stated as Proposition 20 of Book I of Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE).
